topic: Vincent’s lead over Law at Little Round Top

pdf_row.text: Vincent’s lead over Law at Little Round Top | 10 minutes; 15 minutes | 10 minutes | 15 minutes

basis.text: Oates, who commanded the 15th Alabama, wrote in 1905 (printed again by Norton in 1913) that Vincent's brigade reached the ledge ten minutes before his regiment arrived. It is the only figure any witness gives; the reports of 1863 give none and say only that the line was scarcely formed when the attack came.

default.label: 10 minutes: Vincent's brigade reached the ledge ten minutes before Oates's 15th Alabama arrived

animation.note: The picture shows Vincent's line formed on the ledge and the 15th and 47th Alabama coming up to it ten minutes later; the clock time of Vincent's arrival is not set by this row (the reports say about 4 p.m.), and the first attacks on the centre of the brigade come sooner than the flanking column.

default.note: Ten minutes is Oates's estimate, written 42 years after, for the flanking column; fifteen has no source; the other two values stay listed.

positions.label: 10 minutes: Vincent's brigade reached the ledge ten minutes before Oates's 15th Alabama arrived (Oates, 1905)

inference.step: Oates (15th Alabama) wrote in 1905 that Vincent's brigade reached the ledge ten minutes before he did; the reports of 1863 give no figure but say the line was scarcely formed when the first attack came and that the flanking column came later, which agrees with a short lead and does not contradict ten minutes. The figure is taken as Oates's estimate of the lead over the flanking column, not of the first attack.

weighing.summary: Only one witness puts a figure on the lead: Colonel Oates of the 15th Alabama, who wrote in 1905 that Vincent's brigade reached the ledge ten minutes before he did. The reports of 1863 give no figure; they say the line was scarcely formed when the attack came, which fits a short lead without measuring it. No source states fifteen minutes. The 83rd Pennsylvania's clocks give 45 minutes, but its writer later called them wrong, and a Union officer of 1900 says only "a few minutes". Ten is therefore the best-weighted figure, though it rests on one recollection: weighted, inferred. It is the lead over the flanking column that reached the 20th Maine's ledge; by the Union reports the first attack, on the centre of the brigade, came sooner after the line formed.
weighing.who: Oates commanded the 15th Alabama and led the flanking column against the 20th Maine; he is the one man who stood at the ledge when it was reached and also gives the interval. He cannot have seen Vincent's brigade arrive, and he does not say how he knew. Rice (44th New York, then the brigade), Chamberlain (20th Maine), Welch (16th Michigan), Lamont and Woodward (83rd Pennsylvania) were officers of Vincent's brigade on the hill; the chapter of 1900 is by an officer of the brigade staff whose name the volume does not print. Norton, a private of the brigade, reprints Oates and reports Woodward's later correction; Melcher of the 20th Maine repeats a ten-minute halt of the Alabamians.
weighing.when: The reports are of 6 July to 14 August 1863, 4 to 43 days after: the best class of writing there is, but none gives an interval. Oates's figure is of 1905, 42 years after, a recollection; Norton reprints it in 1913. In 1878 Oates wrote that his halt on Round Top lasted "less than ten minutes" and said nothing of Vincent's arrival; in 1885 Melcher printed "some ten minutes" for that halt and said it let Vincent's brigade arrive in time. The figure ten minutes was thus already in print for another interval, and whether the sentence of 1905 rests on a separate memory cannot be told from the record. Where a rejected value has the better class of writing (Woodward, 1863, against Oates, 1905), it loses because its writer withdrew it and three reports of the same brigade (Rice, Welch, Lamont) put the order at about 4 p.m.
weighing.where: Oates was on the Confederate side of the ledge and saw the line only when his regiment was within forty or fifty steps of it. Rice, Chamberlain, Welch, Lamont and Woodward were on the hill with their regiments; Chamberlain's report shows the attack came first on the centre of the brigade and only later, from the foot of Great Round Top, on his left, so the lead over the flanking column is longer than the lead over the first attackers. A lead is also not the same for every regiment of the brigade.
weighing.how_knew: Oates gives no basis for his figure. Rice and Chamberlain knew from their own commands; the writer of 1900 says only that he was on the brigade staff. Woodward gave two clock readings from his own watch; his later admission reaches us through Norton, who quotes a letter of 12 January 1912.
weighing.clock: Oates's figure is a length of time, so no clock enters it. The clock readings of the day cannot decide ten against fifteen: Union reports say about 4 p.m. for the order into position, Norton reads the attack at 4:30 to 5, Bane (4th Texas) has the order to advance at about 4:30 p.m., and Oates's book has the guns opening at about 3:30; each carries an "about" as large as the interval itself. The reported difference of about 20 minutes between the two armies' clocks is not applied.
weighing.independence: One line of knowledge states ten minutes: Oates (book of 1905 and its reprint by Norton; the halt of 1878 and Melcher's ten minutes concern another interval), so the figure is flagged single-source and memoir-only. Fifteen minutes has no witness. The 45 minutes rest on one report that its writer withdrew and that three reports of the brigade (Rice, Welch, Lamont) contradict. The chapter of 1900 and the Park Service ("mere moments", institutional, no source) are voices for a short lead, not for a figure; they pull toward less than ten minutes but cannot outweigh a participant. Norton's remark that the brigade was formed first states no interval.

source_panel_text: Ten minutes: Colonel Oates of the 15th Alabama wrote in 1905 that Vincent's brigade reached the ledge ten minutes before his regiment arrived. The reports of 1863 give no figure, only that the line was scarcely formed when the attack came. No source for fifteen minutes was found. Three other values are listed.

what_would_change_it: A report, diary or letter of 1863 to 1864 that gives clock readings or minutes for both the arrival of Vincent's brigade and the first Confederate contact would replace the recollection of 1905. So would the earlier letters of Oates, Chamberlain or Law (Oates's correspondence to the battlefield commission, the Bachelder papers) if one of them gives the lead, or the sources behind the figures in the plan's two web pages: a figure of fifteen minutes with a source would move the default.
